citations.quote: School of Computer Science, Netanya Academic College 1 University Street, Netanya 4223587, Israel. ahmadjbara@netanya.ac.il

This work presents a tool based on Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) for automating the process of budget calculation - mass, volume, power, and energy - for CubeSat nanosatellites based on user input which can be iteratively finetuned to fit the CubeSat limitations.
This standard describes a range of 1U-12U CubeSats, where a 1U CubeSat is a 10 cm cube and a mass of up to 2 kg.

As CubeSats are modular in their nature, they are composed of many subsystems which are actually built using COTS products, and as such there would be many possible combinations of those products to build the underlying nanosatellite, and hence it is essential to examine these proposed options compliance with the CubeSat budget constraints: mass, volume, power, etc.

Due to its modular structure, a systems engineering approach for designing it is of significant importance, and a ModelBased Systems Engineering (MBSE) option is even much helpful when it comes to breaking down a complex system into smaller manageable parts and dealing with complexity. This approach fits CubeSat usage of COTS and make it easier to customize the underlying system.

In this work, we present an OPM-based budget calculation system model, which caters to process automation, making budget calculating and other related processes explicit, understandable, and usable by the community. In particular, this automation could be useful for rapidly screening combinations of candidate components and then using that screen to increase one's chances of selecting reliable, compatible components from which to build the nanosatellite.

OPM captures and integrates the functional, structural, and procedural aspects of a system in a single unifying model, which is bimodal: models are expressed by both a graphical modality and a textual modality, catering to humans' dual channel processing [9].
The graphical view consists of a set of hierarchically organized, interconnected, and cross-validated Object-Process Diagrams (OPDs).

Computations could be based on predefined mathematical functions, userdefined functions in JavaScript or Python code, or external connection (e.g., MATLAB). Based on these two aspects, OPCloud allows animated execution, where the modeler can execute the model on the basis of informatical objects' values and computations attached to end processes.
However, this work is not meant to be comprehensive in this regard, but rather to use some of the budget calculations to demonstrate a tool that automates the process of budget calculation.
The purpose of this work is two-fold: (1) formally modeling the budget calculating process, and (2) using the model to automate and facilitate this process.

We adopted an OPM model-based systems engineering (MBSE) approach, since, as noted, OPM combines function, structure and behavior in a single diagram kind that uses a minimal set of universal building blocks—objects and processes—and translates on the fly to a subset of natural language. These traits help to build a formal yet simple model that can be easily understood.

Every OPM model starts at level 0 with a system diagram (SD) as depicted in Figure 5, which shows the main process Budget Calculating, represented by an ellipse, surrounded by the objects (rectangles) involved in this process.
Accordingly, the purpose of the Budget Calculating process is to change the Component Selection state from not-accepted to accepted.

Nanosatellite Builder, shown in Figure 5, is an OPM agent—a person or an organization that handles the process to which it is connected. Specifically, this would be the agent who interacts with the system to provide input for the Budget Calculating process.
In this work, for processes, we apply in-zooming, where execution order is necessary, and unfolding, where order is not. As for objects, we apply unfolding to uncover their smaller internal parts.

This diagram shows that the Budget Calculating process is composed of two subprocesses: Budget Quantifying and Decision Making. The former is responsible for calculating budgets and the latter decides whether these calculated budgets comply with the predefined thresholds, and updates the Component Selection state accordingly.
As shown in Figure 10, the Budget Quantifying process is further refined through unfolding into four subprocesses.

Other objects, Antenna System, TRXVU, OBC, and EPS, appear in this diagram, but they were created in different diagrams, and were brought here for their relevance to it (Figure 10). These objects compose the larger object CubeSat NanoSatellite System from Figure 5 which was unfolded into a new diagram as shown in Figure 6.

For example, the Mass Budget Calculating subprocess is responsible for mass calculating. This subprocess is connected to all subsystems by an instrument link (a link that implies 'requires') as it needs their mass. Every subsystem has an attribute that represents its mass. After having this input from all subsystems, the Mass Budget Calculating subprocess calculates the total mass of the nanosatellite and outputs the result into a new object called Mass Budget using a result link (there is an arrow to the direction of this object).

To achieve the second goal of automating the Budget Calculating process for the benefit of any CubeSat nanosatellite builder aspiring to build one, we leverage OPM's extension MAXIM [17], [31] which augments OPM ISO 19450:2015 with the ability to infuse computations and code into the previously qualitative-only OPM model.

As Figure 10 shows, for the Mass Budget Calculating() process to execute, it requires the masses of all subsystems: Antenna System, TRXVU, OBC, and EPS. The masses are entered by the user to the appropriate attributes (objects) within each subsystem object.

citations.quote: The first way of input entering is ahead-of time input which requires that the user enters the data directly into the attribute object as shown in the diagrams of this work. The second way for data entering is run-time input where the user is prompted to insert data while model execution. The third option is a simulated value, where the modeler defines the range of values to select from and the probability distribution. As for output options, the modeler can choose between outputting the results directly into attribute objects as adopted here in this work, or exporting to Excel files.

To verify our model and demonstrate its usage, we use real data taken from ISISPACE—a leading company in the small satellite market [32]. Table 1 shows real data of ISISPACE CubeSat subsystems that allow us to make real calculation for real model verification.

We have proposed a model-based approach that builds on model-based systems engineering using OPM ISO 19450 with computational extensions that are built into OPCloud. The research has achieved its two stated objectives: (1) A detailed OPM model of the budget calculating process and system was constructed, making the process clear and unambiguous; (2) Leveraging the computational capabilities of OPM, the model served as the basis for an executable budget calculating tool.

Specifically, this model-based tool automates and significantly shortens the tedious process of meticulously going over a large and growing number of components that build the underlying nanosatellite, eliminating the need for sifting through a possibly long list of combinations of them.

This feature is of great importance since, as demonstrated, the code embedded in the processes is designed such that the system model can be modified and augmented without the need to alter the code. This facilitates maintaining the system coherent, consistent, and synchronized.

The model-based approach to CubeSats formally explicates the Budget Calculating process and automates it, greatly alleviating the task of determining what components are the best suitable. Beyond streamlining and automating the Budget Calculating process, this work demonstrates the benefits of adopting the OPM model-based systems engineering approach to the domain of CubeSats, which include standardizing and formulating global CubeSats processes and systems, and helping CubeSat professionals navigate their way in the complex, evolving web of CubeSats design.
